title: Diabetic ketoacidosis: the first six hours

bedside.infusions: Fluid {fluidRate} mL/h; insulin {insRate} units/kg/h; potassium {kInRate} mmol/h; dextrose 10% {dex ? 125 : 0} mL/h

secondaryObjectives: Manage a hyperglycemic crisis in order: isotonic fluid resuscitation first, then a continuous IV regular insulin infusion, dextrose added as glucose falls, and overlapping subcutaneous insulin before the infusion stops
Monitor potassium closely during insulin therapy, because insulin and correction of acidosis shift potassium into cells and can cause dangerous hypokalemia

sources.note: Read 2026-11-10 in the Diabetologia copy. DKA: glucose 200 mg/dL or more (or known diabetes), beta-hydroxybutyrate 3.0 mmol/L or more, venous pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18. Isotonic saline or balanced crystalloid at 500-1000 mL/h for the first 2-4 h; fluids alone lower glucose about 50-70 mg/dL per hour. Fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/h. Potassium below 3.5: replace at 10 mmol/h and delay insulin until K is above 3.5; replace once K is below 5.0 to keep 4-5. Glucose below 250 mg/dL: add 5-10% dextrose and reduce insulin to 0.05 U/kg/h, holding glucose about 200 (150-200 per the CCJM summary) until resolution. Capillary glucose every 1-2 h; electrolytes, venous pH and beta-hydroxybutyrate every 4 h. Resolution: ketones below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH 7.3 or more (or bicarbonate 18 or more). Bicarbonate only if pH is below 7.0 (CCJM summary). Hypoglycemia and hypokalemia are common complications of treatment; rapid osmolarity shifts are linked with cerebral edema (under 0.1% of adult events). For HHS, glucose should fall no faster than 90-120 mg/dL per hour.

brief.situation: Handover at 02:00. Bed 9, 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes, 70 kg, two days of vomiting after running out of insulin. Admitted from the ED with DKA. The ED gave 1,000 mL of 0.9% saline over the first hour; saline now runs at 150 mL/h. A DKA protocol is active and the insulin infusion bag is at the bedside, not started. No potassium has been given.
handover: ED labs at 00:50, before any fluid: glucose 520 mg/dL, K 3.6, Na 131, bicarbonate 9, anion gap 26, venous pH 7.12, beta-hydroxybutyrate 6.1 mmol/L.
HR 118, BP 98/58, RR 28 and deep, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2.
Drowsy but oriented. Two peripheral IVs. Foley in, about 60 mL in the last hour.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Glucose checks come back at once; the gas and electrolytes take about 10 minutes. Insulin and potassium take time to act.
Most of the six hours is waiting for the next check: skip ahead, and the skip stops early at an alarm or a result.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends at the 08:00 handover, then a debrief scores what you did.

orderOfCare.question: What do these numbers tell you, and in what order will you treat this patient?

parts.label: What the numbers say
parts.criteria: Names moderate-to-severe DKA (high glucose, raised ketones, low pH and bicarbonate, raised anion gap) and notices that the potassium is below 3.5 despite total-body potassium depletion.
parts.modelAnswer: DKA: glucose about 470, beta-hydroxybutyrate about 6, pH 7.1, bicarbonate about 10, anion gap about 26. Potassium 3.2 is low, and insulin will drive it lower.

parts.label: Order of care
parts.criteria: Fluids first (500-1,000 mL/h), potassium replaced and insulin held until K is above 3.5, then a fixed-rate infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h; hourly glucose; add dextrose and reduce insulin (not stop it) when glucose falls below 250; no bicarbonate at this pH.
parts.modelAnswer: Run fluids at 500-1,000 mL/h now. Give potassium at 10 mmol/h and hold insulin until K is above 3.5, then start insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h and add 20 mmol of potassium per litre. Check glucose hourly and labs every 2 hours. When glucose drops below 250, add dextrose and cut insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h; keep the insulin running until the ketoacidosis clears. Bicarbonate is not indicated at pH 7.1.

source.cite: Umpierrez GE, Davis GM, ElSayed NA, et al. Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report (ADA, EASD, JBDS, AACE, DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275. doi:10.2337/dci24-0032; also Diabetologia 2024, doi:10.1007/s00125-024-06183-8
source.note: Authored window: dextrose within 1 hour of glucose falling below 250 mg/dL, the interval between hourly glucose checks.

noProgress.rationale: Six hours of fluids and potassium with no insulin keeps the patient alive and the potassium safe, but the ketoacidosis has not been treated: delayed care rather than harm within this window.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: read the labs and put the treatment in order

kpis.label: Handover to fluids at 500 mL/h or more
Lowest potassium (mmol/L)
kpis.expert: 3.2 at the start, then 3.5 or more

expertPath.text: Look at the patient, check a glucose, send a venous gas with electrolytes and ketones, and raise the fluid to 1,000 mL/h.
K 3.2: start potassium at 10 mmol/h and hold the insulin. Tell the provider.
Recheck: K 3.5 or more. Start insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h and switch potassium to 20 mmol per litre.
Fluid down to 500 mL/h after the first 2 hours. Glucose hourly; gas and electrolytes every 2 hours.
Glucose below 250: add dextrose 10% at 125 mL/h and cut insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h. Do not stop the insulin; the ketones still need it.
Glucose about 200, K 4-ish, anion gap closing. Plan the overlap to subcutaneous insulin once the DKA has resolved.

arrhythmia.headline: Ventricular arrhythmia from low potassium
arrhythmia.body: The most useful kind of run to learn from. Look at the order: was the potassium known, and 3.5 or more, before the insulin started? Insulin moves potassium into the cells within the hour.

seizure.headline: Seizure from hypoglycemia
seizure.body: The glucose fell too fast and too far. Look at the insulin rate and whether dextrose went in as the glucose passed 250.

resolving.headline: DKA resolving safely
resolving.body: Fluids first, potassium before insulin, a fixed-rate infusion, hourly checks, and dextrose with a lower insulin rate as the glucose fell. That is the expert path.

time_up.headline: Safe at 6 hours, by a slower or rougher route
time_up.body: No one was harmed, but something cost time or safety margin. Check the criteria marked partial or missed, especially the insulin rate, the dextrose time and the lowest potassium.

scoring.modelReasoning: Moderate-to-severe DKA: glucose about 470, ketones about 6, pH 7.1 with a bicarbonate near 10 and a wide anion gap. The potassium of 3.2 is the trap: total-body potassium is depleted, and insulin plus correcting acidosis will drive serum potassium lower, so insulin waits until K is above 3.5 while potassium runs at about 10 mmol/h. Fluids come first at 500-1,000 mL/h. Then fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h with potassium in each litre. Glucose is checked hourly. When it falls below 250, dextrose is added and the insulin reduced, not stopped, because the insulin is there to clear the ketones. Bicarbonate is reserved for pH below 7.0 and would lower potassium further.

kShift.ask: While the gas runs: if K comes back 3.2 and insulin starts now, what will the potassium do over the next hour?
kShift.explain: Fall. Insulin moves potassium into the cells, and correcting the acidosis does too. That is why insulin waits until K is above 3.5 and potassium is replaced first.

source.cite: Umpierrez GE, Davis GM, ElSayed NA, et al. Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report (ADA, EASD, JBDS, AACE, DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275. doi:10.2337/dci24-0032; also Diabetologia 2024, doi:10.1007/s00125-024-06183-8
source.note: Hypokalemia is a common complication owing to intracellular shift of potassium after insulin; below 3.5, delay insulin until K is above 3.5 (read in the Diabetologia copy).

below250.ask: Glucose is heading toward 250 on insulin. When it gets there, what is the plan?

choices.label: Add dextrose and reduce the insulin

below250.explain: Add dextrose and reduce the insulin, to 0.05 units/kg/h in the consensus. The glucose comes down faster than the ketones clear; the insulin is still needed for the ketoacidosis, so the dextrose is there to let it keep running safely.

source.cite: Umpierrez GE, Davis GM, ElSayed NA, et al. Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report (ADA, EASD, JBDS, AACE, DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275. doi:10.2337/dci24-0032; also Diabetologia 2024, doi:10.1007/s00125-024-06183-8
source.note: Once glucose falls below 250 mg/dL, add 5-10% dextrose and reduce the insulin infusion to 0.05 U/kg/h until resolution (read in the Diabetologia copy).

bicarb.ask: The last pH was above 7.0 but still well below 7.3. Should bicarbonate be given?

choices.label: Yes, to correct the acidosis faster

bicarb.explain: No. Fluids and insulin clear the ketoacidosis. Bicarbonate is considered only when the pH is below 7.0, and it pushes potassium into the cells.

source.cite: Rodriguez Alvarez P, San Martin VT, Morey-Vargas OL. Hyperglycemic crises in adults: a look at the 2024 consensus report. Cleve Clin J Med 2025;92(3):152-158. doi:10.3949/ccjm.92a.24089
source.note: Routine bicarbonate is not recommended; consider it only in severe acidosis (pH below 7.0).
